compensating.why: hop 4 always pads the numbers with zeros
hop 3 widens a milliseconds field that follows seconds to three letters
hop 2 pads the numbers whenever the format has a milliseconds letter

ownership_reason: Only the gold sees the tokens of the format, so only it knows that the milliseconds follow seconds and are the fraction of the second; hops 1-4 hold an int breakdown, the format string, the padding flag and the buffer, and no one-line edit there can widen the milliseconds alone (forced padding also pads yyyy, rewriting the S letters does nothing without padding, an int cannot carry leading zeros). The convention is pinned outside the gold: DurationFormatUtils.format, the writer formatPeriod uses, adds 1000 and drops the leading digit for milliseconds written after seconds (lastOutputSeconds), and testFormatPeriodISO expects 'P32Y1M22DT9H11M12.001S' through it; formatDurationISO documents the ISO8601 period format, in which '0.1S' means 100 ms; StopWatch.toString (testStopWatchSimpleGet, '0:00:00.000') and formatDurationHMS (testFormatDurationHMS, '0:00:00.001') pass through the gold with three-letter padding. The gold's javadoc promises the ISO8601 period format for ISO_EXTENDED_FORMAT_PATTERN, which writing 1 ms as '0.1S' violates.
